text: Welcome to Chapter 7, where T-SQL stops being just queries and starts being an actual programming language. We begin with the most basic building block of any language: variables.

Declare, at-sign MinPrice, MONEY — that creates a variable, and you have to give it a data type, just like the ones from Chapter 5. Every single T-SQL variable name starts with the at-sign — that's exactly how SQL Server tells a variable apart from a column or table name at a glance. SET assigns it a value, and from that point on, at-sign MinPrice can be used anywhere a literal value would work — right inside a WHERE condition, here.

SELECT can assign a variable too, and it's especially useful for capturing a query's result. Select at-sign AveragePrice equals average of list price, from Product. This is functionally similar to the scalar subquery from Lesson 52, but split into two steps: capture the value once, into a variable, then use that variable — handy when you need the same computed value more than once in a longer script, without recalculating it every time.

And you don't always need a separate SET line — you can assign an initial value right inside DECLARE itself, and declare more than one variable at once, separated by commas. Min price 100, max price 1000, both set in one line, then used together in a BETWEEN.

DECLARE creates a variable with a type, the at-sign marks it as one, and SET or SELECT assigns its value. Next lesson: batches and GO — what that word you've been typing at the top of every script actually does. See you there.
